To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) we can use implicit human feedback in the form of error-related potentials to augment a DRL agent's learning in Atari-type games, (2) we can do this without requiring any explicit human feedback, (3) we can do so with a simple and effective approach that does not require any specialized hardware, and (4) we can do all of this while maintaining the agent's performance.

we developed an approach that allows us to capture human error-related potentials (ERPs) using EEG, and then use them to accelerate and improve the learning of a DRL agent in an Atari environment, and that this approach is effective for several Atari games.

implicit human feedback can be successfully used to accelerate the learning of DRL algorithms in a variety of Atari games, and the use of implicit human feedback is especially useful for tasks that are difficult to learn with the standard DQN algorithm.

the following questions: How can we use human feedback in DRL? Can we use implicit human reactions to accelerate DRL? Can implicit feedback be used as a reward function in RL?
the following central question: How can we use intrinsic human feedback to accelerate the training and optimize the performance of a deep reinforcement learning algorithm?
the question of whether it is possible to use human feedback to accelerate the training of an agent in an RL setting.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the human implicit feedback, in the form of the error-potentials, can be used as a reward signal to accelerate and optimize DRL algorithms, and that this is a promising direction for further research.

we have developed a system that can capture and decode human implicit feedback (error-potentials) in real-time, and use the feedback to accelerate the learning of a Deep Q-Network (DQN) algorithm in the context of Atari-games.

we have developed a novel method to accelerate the training of a state-of-the-art deep reinforcement learning algorithm by using human implicit feedback in the form of error-related potentials, as a reward augmentation function.

The main takeaway from our work is that

we demonstrate the possibility of using the human's intrinsic reactions (implicit feedback) as an additional source of information for the agent to learn the task more quickly, without any explicit human intervention.

implicit feedback can be a viable alternative to explicit feedback in accelerating the learning of DRL algorithms, and that the human's implicit reactions to the agent behavior are a promising source of implicit feedback.
